versions.description_html:
When a production line halts mid-shift, the real cost isn't just measured on a cloud billing dashboard. It manifests as physical scrap, operators standing idle at a stopped station, and networks flooded with unneeded data. Most cloud-first projects fail because they immediately push everything upward, ignoring the reality of the factory floor where milliseconds and local constraints dictate whether a product makes it or gets scrapped.

THE FACTORY CLOCK: MATCHING WORKLOADS TO TIME HORIZONSA manufacturing plant does not run on a single timeline; it operates on multiple concurrent clocks that handle delay differently. Treating these timelines as a neat hierarchy where slow always means cloud and fast always means edge is a critical design flaw.



  • Milliseconds: Dedicated to control loops and local detection where actions must occur while the process is actively moving.
  • Seconds: Allocated for operator alerts and supervised responses, giving human workers time to interpret conditions safely.
  • Minutes and Hours: Fit shift management, production reviews, line balancing, and MES workflows.
  • Days and Weeks: Designed for maintenance planning, long-term quality trends, capacity analysis, and model training.
SIX QUESTIONS FOR EVERY WORKLOAD PLACEMENTBefore assigning any workload to the edge or the cloud, you must run it through six strict operational criteria to avoid architecture failures during production:



  1. Response Deadline: What is the exact physical consequence if the response arrives late? Does a part move beyond the rejection point, or does the decision just show up later in a report with no physical consequence?
  2. Outage Behavior: Does the function need to survive and continue locally through an unannounced network or firewall drop? You want graceful degradation where production continues within defined local limits.
  3. Data Gravity: How much data is created, and what format does it actually need to take when moving upstream? A design that collects everything forever ends up paying for every unnecessary byte more than once.
  4. Scope: Is the decision constrained to a single sensor, an individual asset, an entire line, or multi-site fleet operations? Local scope favors local placement, while broader scope pushes work upward.
  5. Context: What information (such as work orders, recipes, or material lots) is required to trust the decision without creating brittle live dependencies? Synchronize context as controlled reference data rather than forcing queries to a distant business system for every local choice.
  6. Risk and Governance: Who owns the source data, who approves rule changes, and what audit trail is legally or operationally required? Vague ownership inevitably becomes a production problem later.
THE HYBRID SWEET SPOT: CONTROL AT THE EDGE, HISTORY IN THE CLOUDA resilient architecture does not duplicate the same system on-site and in the cloud. Instead, it roots workloads where they perform best:



  • The Controller: Handles deterministic control, safety loops, and direct machine sequences.
  • The Edge Layer: Collects local signals, enforces bounded rules, buffers events securely during outages, and handles fast inspection and inference.
  • Plant Systems (MES/ERP): Manage local execution, work orders, workflow context, and enterprise business records.
  • Cloud and Fabric: Maintain shared multi-site history, fleet-wide asset analytics, supply chain context, and governed semantic layers.
By respecting these boundaries, you stop treating edge versus cloud as a platform popularity contest and start building a dependable, graceful manufacturing system that protects your plant when it matters most.
